//: Insolvia's brand colours — the ONE place they are written down.
These are OVERRIDES, layered on top of the installed @insolvia-ai/tokens
rather than replacing it. From 0.5.0 the design system's base theme is
deliberately monochrome and states no brand at all: `primary`, `accent`
and `brand` all resolve to neutral-12, and the chrome is steps on the
neutral ramp. That empty seam is the package's intent, not an omission —
so the brand belongs to the consumer, and this file is the consumer.
Only roles Insolvia actually moves appear here. Everything else falls
through to the package, which is what keeps this file short and keeps a
future tokens release able to improve anything we have not claimed:
success / danger            identical in the base already — status
colours are signals, not chrome, and the
base keeps them un-greyed on purpose.
warning                     THE ONE EXCEPTION, and only on dark. The
base's dark `warning` is #D2A857 — the exact
hex this file gives `primary` and `accent`.
A signal that is also the brand's fill is not
a signal: on /cases/:id/packet a `warning`
badge and the `Assemble packet` button came
out the same colour. The rule above assumes
no brand role lands on a status colour; here
one does, so the collision is ours to break
and the override is ours to own. Light needs
nothing — there `primary` is the navy.
dangerText                  the base measures it (6.06:1 light, 6.78:1
dark). Ours would be an unmeasured guess.
overlay* / neutral*         generic utilities, not brand decisions. No
semantic role resolves to a ramp step, so
leaving them costs nothing.
radii                       the base sets every corner to 0 and we keep
it — square IS the new design.
fonts                       the base sets headings in the body sans and
we keep it, for the same reason.
`primaryHover` / `primaryActive` / `accentHover` are DERIVED states, and
they are here for one platform only. On web they are `color-mix()` over
the base role, so overriding `primary` moves them automatically — and the
blends reproduce these exact values, which is why the CSS output omits
them (see tool/render-brand-theme.ts). On React Native they are
pre-computed values with no live blend, so `primary` would move and its
hover would stay behind. `dangerHover` needs no entry: `danger` does not
move, so the base's own derivation is already right.
`bg` / `card` / `surfaceAlt` ARE A LADDER, and dark has to be read as one.
They were once four light-mode hexes doing different jobs — `card` was
light's `ink`, `surfaceAlt` was light's `primary`, `muted` was light's
`line` — which are colours the brand already owned rather than colours
that do the job. The result measured 1.01:1 between `card` and `bg`: a
text input was 0.6% DARKER than the page behind it, so only its border
said it was there, and `surfaceAlt` then jumped back above both. Any edit
here keeps the three monotonically lighter, in that order, with `muted`
landing near 6:1 on `bg` so it stays a step below `ink` rather than a
second shade of white. The base ramp (#111111 / #191919 / #222222) is the
shape to match; ours is the same idea in navy at about 50% saturation,
because a 75%-saturated hue at 9% lightness has nowhere left to go up.
DO NOT hand-copy these values into an app. Every consumer is generated
from this file by `npm run tokens`, and `npm run tokens:check` fails the
build when one has drifted.
The decision, and what to do if a second brand ever appears:
docs/adr/0020-the-brand-is-a-consumer-owned-override.md
